evidence.claim: follows rapids through the Deschutes canyon

evidence.claim: The Lower Deschutes River Back Country Byway follows the river’s east bank for 32 miles.
evidence.quote: Spanning 32 miles along the east bank of the Lower Deschutes Wild and Scenic River

evidence.claim: BLM presents close views of rapids and steep canyon country as the drive’s defining features.
evidence.quote: this back country byway offers close-up views of rapids and steep canyon country.

evidence.claim: Twelve miles between Maupin and Highway 216 near Sherars Falls are paved; the remaining miles are graded gravel suitable for passenger vehicles.
evidence.quote: Twelve paved miles originate from the hamlet of Maupin and connect to state highway 216 near Sherars Falls. The remainder of the byway is surfaced with high-standard gravel, suitable for passenger vehicles.

evidence.claim: Developed recreation sites provide river access throughout the year, with boat launches, day-use areas and campgrounds distributed along the route.
evidence.quote: Twenty-two developed recreation sites offer year-round river access including 4 boat launches, 7 day-use areas, and 10 campgrounds

evidence.claim: Much of the road occupies a former railbed.
evidence.quote: Much of the back country byway was a former railbed

evidence.claim: E. H. Harriman and James J. Hill competed to build routes up the canyon, linking Columbia River mainlines with Central Oregon markets.
evidence.quote: between the rival transportation empires of E. H. Harriman and James J. Hill, as they raced to build routes up the Deschutes River canyon, connecting the mainlines along the Columbia River to the new markets of Central Oregon.

evidence.claim: Harriman’s company built a house at Maupin for the local track-maintenance foreman. Most of its canyon tracks were abandoned in 1936; the road in front of the house now uses the railroad grade.
evidence.quote: Most of the Des Chutes Railroad tracks in the canyon were abandoned in 1936, granting Hill the final victory in the race. The road passing in front of the house utilizes the former railroad grade.

evidence.claim: Harriman’s company built a house at Maupin for the local track-maintenance foreman.
evidence.quote: Harriman's Des Chutes Railroad Company built the house to the Union Pacific Common Standard Plan for buildings (with allowed variations) in 1910.

evidence.claim: for the local track-maintenance foreman
evidence.quote: served as residence for the maintenance of way foreman for the local section of track.

evidence.claim: The station’s depot and maintenance-crew bunkhouse were demolished by 1968, leaving the foreman’s house beside the road.
evidence.quote: The other two buildings of the station (a depot and a bunk residence for the maintenance crew) were demolished by 1968.

evidence.claim: Travel south from the northern terminus at Macks Canyon Campground toward Sherars Falls and the paved connection near Highway 216.
evidence.quote: The byway terminates to the south at Locked Gate Day Use Area and to the north at Macks Canyon Campground.

evidence.claim: the paved connection near Highway 216
evidence.quote: Twelve paved miles originate from the hamlet of Maupin and connect to state highway 216 near Sherars Falls.

evidence.claim: Continue to Maupin, where U.S. 197 crosses the Deschutes, then pass the restored foreman’s house just south of town.
evidence.quote: Road access is provided by U.S. Route 197, which crosses the Deschutes River in town

evidence.claim: the restored foreman’s house just south of town
evidence.quote: Today, the historic Section Foreman's House remains alongside the road just south of Maupin. Open seasonally, the building is restored to historically authentic condition

evidence.claim: The southern stretch ends at Locked Gate Day Use Area.
evidence.quote: The byway terminates to the south at Locked Gate Day Use Area

evidence.claim: Sherars Falls is the Deschutes River’s last waterfall before the Columbia, a drop of about 15 feet near Sherar’s Bridge north of Maupin.
evidence.quote: It is located just north of the city of Maupin on Oregon Route 216 at Sherar's Bridge. It is about 15 feet (4.6 metres) high and is the last waterfall along the Deschutes River before it empties into the Columbia River.

evidence.claim: Tribal fishers use dip nets here to catch salmon and steelhead for subsistence, working from boulders and platforms built by tribal members.
evidence.quote: The waterfall and its surroundings are a well-known location for Tribal fishing for salmon and steelhead for subsistence purposes using the traditional dip-nets technique.

evidence.claim: working from boulders and platforms built by tribal members
evidence.quote: Many fishermen reach from surrounding boulders although several platforms have been erected by the local tribe members.

evidence.claim: The falls take their name from Joseph Sherar, a nineteenth-century wagon-road builder. The crossing upstream was used by wagon trains continuing west to bypass The Dalles.
evidence.quote: It was named after Joseph Sherar, a 19th-century wagon road builder.

evidence.claim: The crossing upstream was used by wagon trains continuing west to bypass The Dalles.
evidence.quote: It is crossed upstream by Sherar's Bridge for Barlow Road. The road is historically the place where wagon trains crossed the Deschutes River and proceeded west in order to bypass The Dalles.

evidence.claim: A ferry crossing survives in Maupin’s sequence of names: Hunts Ferry, then Maupin Ferry, then Maupin.
evidence.quote: Originally named Hunts Ferry after the owner of a ferry on the Deschutes River, the name was changed to Maupin Ferry by town founder William H. Staats.

evidence.claim: then Maupin
evidence.quote: The city's name was shortened to Maupin in about 1909.

evidence.claim: William H. Staats, the town’s founder, made the change to Maupin Ferry. Howard Maupin, the namesake, had a farm and ferry here in the late nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: Maupin is named for Howard Maupin, a pioneer who had a farm and ferry at the town's location in the late 19th century.

evidence.claim: U.S. 197 now crosses the Deschutes in town at one of the few crossings north of Madras. Fishing and rafting connect much of the local economy to the river.
evidence.quote: Road access is provided by U.S. Route 197, which crosses the Deschutes River in town at one of the few places the Deschutes can be crossed north of Madras.

evidence.claim: Fishing and rafting connect much of the local economy to the river.
evidence.quote: Located on the Deschutes River, much of the city's economy is related to the river through outdoor activities, such as fishing and rafting.

evidence.claim: The house beside the road south of Maupin once housed the foreman responsible for maintaining this section of railroad.
evidence.quote: served as residence for the maintenance of way foreman for the local section of track.

evidence.claim: Harriman’s Des Chutes Railroad Company built it in 1910 using a Union Pacific standard plan.
evidence.quote: Harriman's Des Chutes Railroad Company built the house to the Union Pacific Common Standard Plan for buildings (with allowed variations) in 1910.

evidence.claim: It belonged to a three-building country station created during the competition to connect Columbia River rail lines with Central Oregon markets.
evidence.quote: It was one of three buildings in the "country combination station" at Maupin
